extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students (introductory set theory / proofs course)
extracted.subtask_description: Teaching and proving basic cardinality results: definitions (countable/uncountable), Cantor diagonal argument, Cantor's theorem, Cantor–Schröder–Bernstein, comparisons of cardinalities, and constructive injections/bijections between common sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Countable / denumerable set
rubrics_metrics.description: A set is countable if it is finite or denumerable. A set is denumerable if there is a bijection between it and the natural numbers N.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and constructions are used to show sets are denumerable (e.g., Z, N×N via explicit bijections). If B is countable then subsets formed via set operations (e.g., B−A) are countable and unions with disjoint countable sets remain countable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncountable set
rubrics_metrics.description: A set is uncountable if it is not countable (i.e., there is no bijection with N).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show uncountability, show no bijection from N to the set exists; the textbook proves (0,1) is uncountable and deduces R is uncountable because (0,1) ⊆ R. Use proof by contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decimal expansion facts (uniqueness and handling duplicates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every rational number has a repeating decimal expansion; some rationals have two expansions (e.g., 1/2 = 0.5000... = 0.4999...). A rational p/q (reduced) has two expansions iff q is a product of powers of 2 and 5. Every irrational has a unique (non-repeating) decimal expansion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When listing real numbers in (0,1), choose the expansion that ends in all zeros to make the representation unique for rationals. When constructing counterexamples (e.g., diagonal argument), avoid using digits 9 (and often 0) to circumvent the two-expansions pathology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor diagonal argument (1891) for (0,1) uncountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume there is a bijection f:N→(0,1) and list the decimal expansions x1,x2,.... Form the diagonal ∆ whose nth digit is the nth digit of f(n), then construct z whose nth digit differs from ∆'s nth digit (avoiding 9s/0s). Because z differs from every f(n) in the nth digit, z is not on the list, contradicting bijectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make diagonal ∆ = 0.d1d2d3..., set z's digits so each digit of z is different from the corresponding digit of ∆ (take digits 1 or 2, for example). Avoid digits 9 to prevent duplicate decimal representations; when listing, use expansions that end in zeros for rationals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule: When listing decimals, pick expansion ending with zeros
rubrics_metrics.description: When constructing a list of real numbers (e.g., for Cantor's diagonal) if a number has two expansions, write down the expansion that ends in all zeros.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This convention ensures each real in the list has a unique chosen decimal expansion and avoids ambiguity with numbers that also have an expansion ending in repeating 9s.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: |A| ⩽ |B| and |A| < |B| via injections
rubrics_metrics.description: Write |A| ⩽ |B| if there is an injection from A to B. Write |A| < |B| to mean |A| ⩽ |B| and |A| ≠ |B| (i.e., there is an injection from A to B but no bijection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This translates finite-set intuition about cardinalities to infinite sets. Use injections to establish 'less than or equal' relations and show nonexistence of bijections to get strict inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor's theorem: |A| < |P(A)|
rubrics_metrics.description: For any set A, |A| ⩽ |P(A)| (there is an injection f(a)={a}) and there is no bijection from A to P(A); hence |A| < |P(A)|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof that no surjection g:A→P(A) can exist: define G = {x∈A | x∈g(x)} and B = {x∈A | x∉g(x)}; B∈P(A) so by surjectivity some q∈A satisfies g(q)=B, leading to contradiction whether q∈B or q∉B. The argument is presented as a contradiction reminiscent of Russell's paradox.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary: infinitely many distinct infinities via iterated power sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying Cantor's theorem iteratively yields |N| < |P(N)| < |P(P(N))| < ... hence there are infinitely many different infinite cardinalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with any infinite set (e.g., N or R) and take successive power sets to obtain strictly larger cardinalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor–Schröder–Bernstein theorem (CSB)
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is an injection f:A→B and an injection g:B→A then there is a bijection h:A→B; equivalently, if |A| ⩽ |B| and |B| ⩽ |A| then |A| = |B|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the bijection by analyzing forward/backward 'trajectories' under f and g: classify trajectories into types (infinite line, loop, forward infinite with backward stuck in A, forward infinite with backward stuck in B). Define h(x)=f(x) on 'good' trajectories and h(x)=g^{-1}(x) on 'bad' ones. Prove h is injective and surjective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique: constructing injections/bijections between intervals and sets
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove equinumerosity of common sets, construct explicit injections (and apply CSB if needed). Examples: identity map (0,1)→[0,1), g(x)=0.1(1+x) maps [0,1)→(0,1), f(x)=1−x maps [0,1)→(0,1], etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes explicit bijections are given; other times show injections both ways and invoke CSB. For (0,1) and [0,1) special rationals of form n/(n+1) are treated separately (explicit piecewise definitions) to achieve bijectivity/surjectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing injections between P(N) and R (showing |P(N)| = |R|)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define g: P(N)→R by mapping X⊆N to y with decimal digits yn=1 if n∈X and yn=0 if n∉X. Define h:[0,1)→P(N) by mapping decimal expansion 0.x1x2x3... to the set {x1,10x2,100x3,...}. These give injections both ways, so by CSB |P(N)| = |R|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure uniqueness of decimal expansions by avoiding those that end in infinite 9s; argue distinct inputs give distinct outputs by examining differing digits/indices; compose with bijections between R and [0,1) if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor's first proof of uncountability using the least upper bound property
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume a bijection g:N→[a,b] produces a sequence x_n of distinct reals. Construct nested intervals (a_n,b_n) by repeatedly choosing the first two sequence elements inside the current interval; form monotone bounded sequences a_n (increasing) and b_n (decreasing). Using the LUB property and convergence of monotone bounded sequences, obtain a limit point q that cannot be any x_n, contradicting surjectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This proof relies on the completeness (least upper bound) axiom of R and the lemma that increasing bounded sequences converge. Handle the finite termination case separately (if the nested intervals stop, any point inside the final interval is not on the list).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuum hypothesis (statement and status)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjecture: There is no set A such that ℵ0 < |A| < c (no cardinality strictly between countable and continuum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically central: Gödel (1931) showed it cannot be disproved from standard axioms of set theory (ZFC); Cohen (1963) showed it cannot be proved from ZFC — i.e., it is independent of ZFC.

rubrics_metrics.name: General proof strategies for cardinality comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Use explicit injections to show |A| ⩽ |B|, show nonexistence of bijection (often by diagonal or contradiction) to get strict inequality, or produce injections both ways and apply CSB to obtain equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical tools: explicit formulae for functions, diagonalization, partitioning sets, pigeonhole arguments for finite cases, and careful handling of special elements (e.g., rationals with two decimal expansions). Many exercises ask for explicit bijections (not tables) and for proving injectivity/surjectivity rigorously.
